rationale: B wins because it has adult discipline: it turns the rollout into usable beats while gating every claim with proof, especially "whether every store has repair technicians on site or is a drop-off point." A has bigger swings, but "As outdoor gear floods secondhand apps" smuggles in an unsourced market premise, and "public retailers can't easily replicate" is a thesis it has not earned. B is less dazzled by its own cleverness, which is usually where the money is.
gaps_in_A: "public retailers can't easily replicate" overclaims the competitive argument. The update says REI is a co-op, not that public retailers cannot scale resale or repair.
"because there are no external shareholders demanding margin protection" is a tidy MBA sentence, not a supplied fact. Frame it as a question for analysts, not as the spine of the angle.
"As outdoor gear floods secondhand apps" invents the market condition the angle depends on. A knows it needs data later, but the headline has already spent the fact it does not have.
"expanding a program that requires trained repair technicians" assumes store-level skilled roles before proving whether stores repair on site, retrain staff, or route gear elsewhere.
gaps_in_B: "resale and repair stop being a side channel and become something every store has to staff and stock" slightly outruns the facts. B correctly asks for the operational proof, but the angle should not state the staffing model first.

"the co-op had its best year for members" risks laundering "largest-ever dividend" into broader financial performance. It may be true; it is not proven without total, per-member, and prior-year figures.
"Your old tent now has a trade-in price at the local REI" is vivid, but it invents a specific accepted item. Fine as a working headline, dangerous if tents are excluded or condition-limited.
